Lessons.Title: Finding Unknown Inputs
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: use graphs and function notation to identify input values that produce a specified output of a quadratic function; understand that several inputs may share one output. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 1 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/1/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/1/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source opens by reading quadratic flight graphs rather than insisting on formal symbolic solving.

Original invented arch-height model h(t)=16−(t−3)² metres for t∈[0,7] seconds. It rises to a maximum16m at t3 then falls. At t0 and t6, output is7m: h(0)=16−9=7 and h(6)=16−9=7. This is a graph interpretation, not two separate flights.

To find which time corresponds to height7, intersect the parabola with horizontal line h=7. Its intersections are (0,7) and (6,7). The domain matters: the algebraic graph extends to other t values, but negative elapsed time would be invalid in a real launch. If the model has measurement uncertainty, a hand-drawn crossing may only approximate a value; this exact first-party model is constructed for exact checks.

Student task: graph original model, mark vertex and both points at height7, compare h(1) and h(5), and explain why a fixed output can correspond to two distinct inputs without violating function uniqueness. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for graph, two correct inputs, context restrictions and complete interpretation.

V12 source-aligned new independently authored GEOMETRIC CONSTRAINT task: a rectangular picture measures8 by5 inches, and a uniform nonoverlapping frame of border thickness x inches surrounds all four edges. The frame material covers 30 square inches. Outer dimensions are (8+2x) by (5+2x), so the necessary area equation is (8+2x)(5+2x)−8×5=30, equivalently4x²+26x=30. A border thickness of x=1 gives outer rectangle10×7 area70, picture area40, and frame area30. Negative x is impossible. Let students propose and explain this equation before completing formal quadratic solving techniques.

V12 geometric diagram task: draw an 8×5 inner rectangle centered in a 10×7 outer rectangle for x=1, label four strips of thickness1 and the corner regions; explain why the frame area is outer area minus picture area. Compare with the existing first-party flight example h(t)=16−(t−3)^2, which yields height7 at t0 and6, to explain that the same target output may have more than one input. The publisher uses a launched-object context and a physical framing-cut activity; independent values avoid copying the paper cut-out dimensions.

Draft teacher assessment0–2 each for labelled original picture/frame diagram, exact geometric area equation, check at x1 with units/domain, and interpretation of context roots/unknown inputs. This is evidence of an authored task, not of actual cutting, authenticated teacher grading, or a student solution.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unknown input
KeyConcepts.Definition: To find a time for a target output, locate intersections with a horizontal target line.

KeyConcepts.Title: Function uniqueness
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each input has one output, but multiple inputs can share an output.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Separate equal y-values from equal x-values.

KeyConcepts.Title: Physical domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use only elapsed times supported by the situation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Apply t≥0 and end of modeled flight.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a function cannot give the same output twice
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Uniqueness restricts outputs per input, not inputs per output.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Keeping negative elapsed times as valid physical solutions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Some equations have extraneous context solutions.

SummaryPoints: A horizontal target line may cross a quadratic graph twice.
The invented flight reaches height7m at times0 and6s.
Equal outputs at different inputs do not violate function definition.
Teacher reviews graphical interpretation and restrictions.
